Chapter 4 — Putting Numbers on the Picture

Causal Analysis in Public Health Management | BK Advisors

Matthew Luke Kuch | BK Advisors

2026-04-18

Meet Joyce

Joyce, 41, midwife at a rural facility in Mwanza Region, Tanzania (a composite drawn from the Tanzania Service Provision Assessment 2014/15 — the details are real, the name is not)

Joyce has delivered hundreds of babies in her career.

Last week she opened her stockroom and counted. Of the 100 women she has delivered in the last twelve months, 55 came in with at least one major risk factor — bleeding history, anaemia, prior caesarean, or eclampsia signs (consistent with TSPA 2014/15 facility-level data).

Of those 55, 6 ended badly — either the mother or the baby did not come home.

The question: A new mother walks in tomorrow with anaemia. What is the chance she has a bad outcome — and how do we get an answer that is actually useful to Joyce, in plain numbers, not in formulas?

And here is the puzzle

Tanzania’s national surveys give us numbers like “the maternal mortality ratio is 524 per 100,000 live births” (WHO, 2017).

But Joyce does not deliver 100,000 births. She delivers about 100 a year.

A number that is right at the country level can be useless at the bedside. What we need is a way to take the picture from Chapters 2 and 3 and turn each arrow into a number Joyce can actually use.

Counts before formulas

Forget probability for a minute

People say “the probability is 0.06” and most of the room glazes over.

People say “6 out of 100” and everybody gets it.

Natural frequencies — counts out of a round number — are how human brains were built to think about chance. We are going to use them for the entire chapter.

Probability is just frequency in disguise. If you ever get lost in this chapter, translate everything back into “X out of 100”.

Joyce’s last 100 mothers

Out of the 100 mothers Joyce delivered in the last year:


Anaemia No anaemia Total
Bad outcome 5 1 6
Good outcome 35 59 94
Total 40 60 100

That is the whole picture in one table. Every row, every column, every cell — people, not probabilities.

Reading the table

  • Out of every 100 mothers Joyce sees, 40 have anaemia.
  • Out of those 40 with anaemia, 5 have a bad outcome. That is 5 out of 40 — or about 1 in every 8.
  • Out of the 60 without anaemia, only 1 has a bad outcome. That is 1 in 60.
  • A mother with anaemia is roughly 8 times more likely to end badly than a mother without.

Notice what we just did. We answered Joyce’s question — “a new mother walks in with anaemia, what is the chance?” — in counts. No formulas.

Putting counts on the picture

From a chain to a lookup table

Remember Faith’s bleeding chain from Chapter 3? (bleeding → family decides → permission → motorbike → arrives → survives)

Each arrow on that chain can carry a lookup table — a small box of counts that says “out of every 100 women who reach this point, X go this way and Y go that way”.

A picture with a lookup table on every arrow has a name. We call it a Bayesian network.

Don’t be intimidated by the name. It is just a picture from Chapter 2 with counts attached.

Joyce’s tiny picture, with the table on it


Anaemia → Bad outcome

Bad outcome Good outcome Total
Anaemia 5 35 40
No anaemia 1 59 60

Two boxes. One arrow. One lookup table. That is the smallest possible picture-with-numbers — and it already answers Joyce’s question.

Why this is a big deal

Once an arrow has a lookup table on it, you can ask the picture new questions — running the arrow in both directions.

  • Forward — a mother walks in with anaemia. What’s the chance of a bad outcome? 5 out of 40 = roughly 1 in 8.
  • Backward — a bad outcome happened. What’s the chance the mother had anaemia? 5 out of 6, because 5 of the 6 bad outcomes were in anaemia mothers.
  • Comparison — does anaemia matter? 1 in 8 versus 1 in 60 — anaemia mothers are about 8 times more likely to have a bad outcome.

Same table, three different questions, three different answers. The picture with numbers can answer questions the picture without numbers cannot.

Where do the numbers come from?

  • The facility logbook. Joyce literally counted the last 100 mothers.
  • The DHIS2 database. Tanzania’s national health information system — public, free, district-level data on bleeding rates and maternal outcomes.
  • The Service Provision Assessment. A survey of facility readiness done every few years — anaemia screening rates, drug availability, staffing.
  • The interviews from Chapter 3. Mary, Lokol, and Esther can give you rough fractions even when the database cannot.

You almost never need to estimate a number perfectly. You need to estimate it well enough that the picture starts giving useful answers. Better to be roughly right than precisely wrong.

Three quiet warnings

Warning 1 — Your numbers will be local

Joyce’s 100 mothers are not the same as Mwanza Region’s 1,000 mothers, which are not the same as Tanzania’s 1.8 million births a year.

The lookup table is local. Use it locally. When you need national numbers, get national counts.

Warning 2 — Small counts lie

Joyce had 6 bad outcomes out of 100. That sounds solid. But 6 is a small number.

If two of those bad outcomes had been on different days, the picture would have looked very different.

With small counts, your numbers are noisy. We mark this on the picture by putting a range on each cell — not just “5 out of 40” but “5 out of 40, somewhere between 2 and 10.”

Warning 3 — Numbers can hide a missing arrow

You can put a beautiful lookup table on every arrow you drew — and still be wrong, because there is an arrow you forgot to draw.

The picture has to be right first. A wrong picture with perfect numbers is worse than a right picture with rough numbers. Always come back to Chapter 2’s grammar before you start counting.

Try it yourself

You are the analyst

scenario

In a Tanzanian district, 100 women were tested for HIV during antenatal care last month. 20 tested positive. Of those 20, 3 had a low-birth-weight baby. Of the 80 who tested negative, 6 had a low-birth-weight baby.

Build a tiny lookup table. Then answer: a new HIV-positive mother is how many times more likely to have a low-birth-weight baby than an HIV-negative mother?

Hint: count the rates first — 3 out of 20 versus 6 out of 80 — then divide them.

Looking ahead

In Chapter 5, you will take a picture-with-numbers like Joyce’s and learn what to do when new evidence arrives.

A new test result comes back. A new survey lands on your desk. A new patient walks in. The picture does not get thrown out — it gets updated. That is what “Bayesian thinking” actually means in plain language.

Further reading

The data behind Joyce’s story

  • Tanzania Service Provision Assessment (TSPA) 2014/15 — the most recent national facility-level survey. Open-access at dhsprogram.com.
  • WHO, 2017 — Trends in maternal mortality: 1990 to 2015. The source for Tanzania’s maternal mortality ratio. Open-access.
  • DHIS2 Tanzania — national health information system, district-level dashboards at moh.go.tz.

If you want to go deeper

  • Ryall, M. D. & Bramson, A. L. (2014) — Inference and Intervention. Routledge. Chapter 5 walks through lookup tables and conditional probability tables for business decisions; the same machinery applies here.
  • Gigerenzer, G. (2002) — Calculated Risks. The book that convinced every doctor in Europe to teach probability in natural frequencies instead of percentages.

The one thing to remember

A picture from Chapter 2 + a lookup table on every arrow = a Bayesian network.

That is all there is to it. The picture tells you the structure. The counts tell you the strengths. Together, they answer questions neither could answer alone.
